name: The Hours We Invented: A History of Keeping Time
description: Shadows, dripping water, swinging weights and vibrating atoms: how humans learned to count the days and divide them, from Stonehenge to satellites.

checkpoints.name: Sun, moon and water
checkpoints.note: Stonehenge and the Egyptian and Maya calendars followed the sky, sundials and water clocks split the day, and Rome's calendar was tidied by Caesar into the Julian year.

checkpoints.name: Sacred and mechanical
checkpoints.note: Calendars of faith, such as the Hebrew and Islamic, were fixed, Dionysius proposed counting from Christ's birth, and the verge escapement made mechanical clocks possible.

checkpoints.name: Pendulum and reform
checkpoints.note: Hourglasses and clocks spread through towns. Galileo studied the pendulum, Huygens built the first accurate pendulum clock, and a papal reform created the Gregorian calendar.

checkpoints.name: Longitude and order
checkpoints.note: Harrison's marine chronometer solved the problem of finding longitude at sea. The French tried decimal time, the metric system arrived, and railways forced standard time and a prime meridian.

checkpoints.name: Atoms and satellites
checkpoints.note: Quartz clocks, then atomic clocks, set a steadier beat than the Earth itself. The SI second, Coordinated Universal Time and GPS satellites now keep the whole planet in step.
